thread.title: Don't Sell Micron Technology Because Of Trade War - Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) | Seeking Alpha

author: Kwan-Chen Ma
title: Don't Sell Micron Technology Because Of Trade War - Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Since March, President Trump said that his administration will levy a 25% tariff on "about $150 billion" worth of 1,300 Asian (China, Japan, Korea and Taiwan) imported technological goods. Where exactly the 25% levies will fall is still unknown, but the focus will obviously reflect the Administration's concerns about China's aggressive moves to acquire and obtain new technology in areas such as semiconductors, computing, and manufacturing.
China immediately responded and followed through with its own tariffs on 128 U.S. products, mainly agricultural goods, with an import value of $3 billion. It is not yet known whether the US technology sector will be the next target of further Chinese retaliation, but it is likely given the large orders Chinese manufacturers place with Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU ), Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ), Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), and other US chipmakers. However, China's choice of the tech "hit list" becomes a delicate one since many U.S. hardware makers rely on Chinese contract manufacturers. Therefore, any technology tariffs would make such measure a double-edged sword.
There could be more complications for Micron in the foreseeable future. Since the U.S. tariffs tech hit list is not out yet, if Chinese manufactured chips and electronic components make the list, hardware makers and component distributors will be worse off. If tariffs are levied on finished goods from contract manufacturers, then Micron will be hurt. As Micron has more than 30% of supplies imported from Asia and 77% of revenue from the same region, the closely integrated relationship may become hardly distinguishable when it comes to U.S. tariffs and China retaliation tariffs.
As semiconductor is the fastest growing technology focused industry in China, it would seem as if Micron is more vulnerable to both Trump's tariffs and China's retaliation. Because of this consideration, I have estimated Micron's exposure to both tariffs. The U.S. tariffs exposure is measured by the company's cost distribution of its Asian suppliers, while the China tariffs exposure is measured by the revenue distribution of its Asian customers.
Level-1 Asian Suppliers "Level-1" suppliers are the top 9 Asian companies directly providing products to Micron. They may take the full impact of the 25% US imported tariffs. If Micron’s suppliers make the list, Micron may have to pay the additional cost to the level-1 suppliers if they choose to pass the entirety of the tariffs to U.S. importers. In Figure 1, I identified Micron’s top 9 largest Asian suppliers with each of its cost contribution to the company. It is interesting to note that four Taiwanese firms represent 5.53% Micron's costs of goods sold, while the Chinese suppliers have virtually no exposure. The sharp difference between Taiwan and China poses important implications. First, if Trump tariffs are only directed at China, it appears to be ineffective, at least to Micron. As the data indicates, Micron is practically not affected by the U.S. tariffs targeted at Chinese suppliers.
"Made in China" vs. "Made by China" Even if Micron does not have Chinese suppliers on whom U.S. tariffs can be directly levied, one potential complication is whether tariffs will be levied on tech goods manufactured in China (made in China) or on tech goods manufactured by Chinese firms (made by China). This will be an important factor since most Taiwanese manufacturers have significant production facilities in China. In Table 1, the import cost exposure for each scenario is identified and calculated. For Micron, the exposure can be around 5%-6%. Applying 25% tariffs to the exposed cost ratio represents the increase in cost. Micron is expected to have a cost increase no more than 1.5%, depending on how U.S. tariffs are applied. Most importantly, it should be pointed out that since Micron only has 13.6% U.S. sales (Table 1), the net cost increase for Micron will be 0.20% - hardly an alarming increase.
Note that the above estimates are based on an unlikely twist that Trump's undisclosed hit list may grossly classify Taiwan as part of China, or Greater China area. However, such a scenario may be theoretically possible, but likely simply from the political reality in that region. President Trump has made his intention of separating Taiwan from China very clear by calling the Taiwanese "President" at the first day in White House.
Level-2 Asian Suppliers "Level-2" suppliers are any Micron suppliers, Asian or not, who provide Asian products to Micron from their own Level-1 Asian suppliers. The need for the identification is that Level-2 suppliers will also pass their increased cost from their Level-1 Asian suppliers to Micron. To make it a bit clearer, I illustrated a real example below for the different cost contribution from both Level 1 and Level 2 suppliers.
In Figure 2, Powertech is a Level-1 (3.55%) U.S. supplier to Micron, and Shenzhen Kaifa Tech is a Level-1 (4.5%) supplier to Powertech. Although Powertech itself is not subject to U.S. tariffs, it will still pass the cost increase (4.5% cost exposure) from its Level-1 Asian supplier's U.S. tariffs burden to Micron. There may be some remote chance that Micron may be exposed to some Level-2 Asian suppliers even if there is no transaction between the two. Though, the derived effect should be minimal. Thus, in a way, Micron may be exposed to the Level-2 Asian suppliers. In short, the nine Level-2 suppliers may add another 0.3% to Micron's Level-1 suppliers' 5.53% cost exposure.
The supply tree can theoretically go on forever, that is, the imposition of 25% tariffs serves more like a multiplier which has a far-reaching impact and not just confined within only direct Asian suppliers. The good news is that after Level-2 suppliers, the actual cost increase will quickly converge to a negligible level. For all practical purposes, Micron's U.S. tariffs exposure on cost should be confined within Level-1 and Level-2 Chinese suppliers only, which is around 6% at best. As Trump's tariffs are only directed to the tech goods made by Chinese firms, the cost increase for Micron will be negligible, at a level no more than 1.5%.
China's Retaliation Tariffs Given the strong and surprising stance of Trump's tariffs, there will be and there have been retaliations from the targeted countries, i.e., China, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan. So, while Micron may not be significantly affected by Chinese retaliation on the supplier side, it has a much larger stake on the Asian revenue side. On this front, Micron may be vulnerable than most since it has revenue exposure from both the Greater China region and from China in particular (Figure 3). Specifically, I further identified Micron's Asian customers and their revenue contributions. The customer is considered "qualified" if its revenue contribution can be individually identified. The "unqualified" customer is the one that its revenue is estimated approximately based on its market capitalization. Micron has around 13.59% of Asian qualified revenue. More importantly, Micron has about 5% revenue from China directly (Lenovo and Huawei).
Realistically, the most likely country to impose a retaliation tariff is China. This is because China is the main target of Trump's tariffs. At this point, Micron has around 5% China “qualified” revenue and maybe 10% “unqualified” revenue exposure at risk if Trump's tariffs are restricted to China only and there is a China retaliation tariff directly to the U.S. Given the relatively small revenue portion that each firm is exposed to China retaliation tariffs, even with a similar 25% tariff levied on the U.S. revenue, it is hard to imagine that there is a significant loss in revenue for Micron. Again, considering the political reality in that region, it is less likely that Japan, Korea, and Taiwan will join suit with China to organize a coordinated tariff in retaliation.
Finally, many have considered that the recent exchanges of tariff threats between the U.S. and China are no more than political posture and reelection campaign rhetoric. Just days after Trump's announcement, China has taken off 201 tariffs on Apple after Apple donated $400 million to poor Chinese students. According to some reports, China has offered to increase the purchase of U.S. semiconductor chips, replacing offerings from South Korea and Taiwan. Thus, it stands to reason that the tariffs' impact on Micron's revenue and cost should be measured and contained.
With less than 2% negative impact on Micron’s top and bottom lines, Micron's near 20% losses in market capitalization, amid Trump’s $150 billion tariffs announcements, seem excessive.
